Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung, Vatican says

The Vatican said the pope woke up normally after the operation and would remain in hospital for several days to recover.

Pope Leo arrives at Gemelli Hospital ahead of the pontiff's surgery to remove a lung nodule, in Rome, Italy on Oct 13, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Ciro de Luca)

ROME: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday (Oct 13), the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff. The pope has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said. Pope Leo was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent routine health check. The pope's lead surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr Luigi Carbone, said in a statement that the procedure lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications.

"In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," they said, making clear that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue. Human lungs have five lobes - three in the right lung and two in the left. A medical expert said that in order to assess the pope's case, they would need to know the size of the tumour and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide. "While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment," said Dr Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of haematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital. "If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative," he told Reuters. "But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis." RESTING IN HIS HOSPITAL ROOM The pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the medical bulletin said. The Vatican said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and all his public events have been cancelled until Oct 20. Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1pm local time in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9km north of the Vatican to the Gemelli.

Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted "Auguri" (best wishes), and headed in via the main entrance. Leo, elected by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues. The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025. Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. TYPHOID FEVER The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval. Pope Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalised. He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as pope, in a book for Penguin Peru. Pope Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that "We need you here (on Earth)", he said. "I never looked back," said Leo.

Source: Reuters/fs/dc

MOSCOW: Russia 's Federal Security Service said it detained a Japanese journalist accused of gathering information on Russia 's defence capabilities, news agencies reported on Tuesday (Oct 13). FSB said the journalist for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper had been detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region before he planned to leave Russia , and was subsequently transferred to custody in Moscow, Interfax reported. Russia n state TV showed a man lying on a floor and handcuffed by three masked men in black uniform. A voice behind the scene tells him he is suspected of spying . TV also showed him boarding a plane accompanied by two FSB servicemen, then in a cage on trial in a Moscow court, which authorised his custody for nearly two months.

Russia regards Japan as an "unfriendly" country as it has joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine. Japan's embassy in Moscow did not answer phone calls out of business hours. Russia and Japan never signed a formal World War Two peace treaty, with the main obstacle being an unresolved territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Russia n President Vladimir Putin visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an uproar in Japan. Tokyo has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine. One of the most prominent cases of a foreign journalist arrested in Russia was the detention of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich in 2023. He was found guilty of espionage by a Russia n court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.

THE HAGUE: Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay urged the United States on Tuesday (Oct 13) to return to its traditional role of defender of human rights and liberator for the rest of the world amid a US campaign to undermine the International Criminal Court.  "My message is: 'You have to get back to playing your serious role as a leader, playing a liberatory role for the rest of the world'," Pillay, 85, told Reuters in The Hague, where she is currently a judge at the United Nations' highest legal body, the International Court of Justice.   Hours after Pillay was announced as the winner of the Peace Prize on Friday, the United States announced sweeping sanctions aimed at her former employer, the International Criminal Court.  She said the timing of the sanctions, an unprecedented attack on an institution founded by international treaty, right after her Nobel Prize win could not be coincidental.

"I think it's very unfortunate. However, the plans of targeting international criminal justice through the ICC were brewing all the time," Pillay said. "That's why the first thing I did when I returned from Nuremberg to The Hague is to go to the staff of the ICC to show solidarity for their work in promoting international criminal justice and to protect those who've already been sanctioned." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday called the ICC a "rogue court" that would never be allowed to prosecute Americans. The new sanctions were suspended for six months, and included some other exemptions for transactions for telecoms, software, payment of pensions and transactions related to detainees. The US has long been hostile to the court, and especially the ICC statute that says it has jurisdiction not only over nationals of member states but also over others alleged to have committed atrocity crimes on the territory of member states.

SOFIA: Eleven sailors were missing at sea on Tuesday (Oct 13) from a ship sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria, the second deadly sinking of a cargo vessel in the area in a week, prompting Bulgaria to summon Russia's ambassador. Two cargo ships were hit by drones overnight and one was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation". There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the incidents. "This is absolutely unacceptable - another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters," Radev said in a televised address.

The attacks were also condemned by Ukraine and the EU. "The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on X. "Those responsible should be held accountable." Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X on Tuesday that the strike "once again demonstrates Moscow's deliberate disregard for civilian lives". "The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage," he said. BLACK SEA SHIPPING DRAWN INTO WAR Bulgarian officials said five crew members had been rescued but 11 were still listed as missing from the ship which sank off the coast of the village of Krapets. Bulgarian media identified the vessel as the cargo ship Azov Concord. Its Türkiye-based manager was not immediately available for comment. Another ship, the Chelsea 3 sailing under Maltese flag, was also hit by three drones overnight, Bulgarian officials said. All crew from that ship - seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis - were rescued and none seriously injured. A week ago nine Syrian sailors and one Egyptian were lost at sea from a ship that sank when hit by drones in Bulgaria's Black Sea exclusive economic zone. Another ship was also hit that night but the crew was rescued. More than four and a half years into the war that Moscow launched with its full-scale invasion in 2022, Black Sea shipping has increasingly been drawn into a prolonged battle of economic endurance. Ukraine and Russia are both among the world's largest exporters of grain. Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Ukraine to rely increasingly on river ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania. Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly targeted Russian grain-exporting ships in other parts of the Black Sea and the Azov Sea at the mouth of the Don River.

TAIPEI: The Trump administration opposes "coercion and aggression" by China against countries for exercising their sovereign rights, the US State Department said, after Beijing sanctioned Belizean and Paraguayan ministers over their ties to Taiwan. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said in response that the United States should "stop sending the wrong signals to Taiwan separatist forces". Paraguay and Belize are two of just 12 countries to maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. China says Taiwan is one of its provinces with no right to behave like a state, a view Taipei's government strongly rejects. The sanctions are largely symbolic because ministers from Taiwan's diplomatic allies generally do not travel to China. Beijing has previously imposed similar measures mainly on Western politicians for their support of democratically governed Taiwan.

"The Trump administration opposes coercion and aggression by China against countries in our hemisphere for exercising their sovereign rights," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement. Pigott cited previous comments by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the US "will not allow our region to become a base of operation for adversaries, competitors, and rivals to threaten our security or undermine our partnerships". "We stand with our friends and partners, including Taiwan, to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values," Pigott added. The United States is Taiwan's most important international backer, despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Washington has been concerned not only by Beijing's efforts to win over Taiwan's remaining allies, but also by attempts to increase its influence in Latin America.

Related:

TAIWAN'S VISIBILITY "GROWING HIGHER" Speaking on Tuesday (Oct 13) to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi said China was extending "transnational repression" to Taiwan's allies. "Taiwan's international visibility is growing higher and higher, and they will be kept busy by this fact," Chen said, referring to China. "Do they plan to sanction the whole world?" Taiwan Premier Cho Jung-tai said Beijing had no right to interfere in the domestic affairs of, or influence the diplomacy of, any sovereign and independent state, "including the Republic of China", referring to the island's formal name. "At the same time, we will resist any expansion of hegemony or authoritarianism," he added, also speaking at parliament. China has stepped up pressure on Taiwan's remaining diplomatic allies to sever ties with Taipei. The last country to do so was the tiny Pacific Island nation of Nauru, in 2024. Honduras ended its decades-long ties with Taiwan in 2023.

Source: Reuters/ec

SEOUL: South Korea's ambassador to the United States said Washington had raised concerns about intelligence cooperation between the allies and that Seoul had not yet fully addressed US expectations, Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday (Oct 13). Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha told a South Korean parliamentary audit in Washington that intelligence sharing was the most difficult issue in bilateral relations, according to Yonhap. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised the matter during talks with South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun last month, Kang said. Kang did not detail Washington's concerns, but said communication between the two countries' intelligence agencies was continuing and had made progress.

The ambassador also said access to senior White House officials had been limited, according to the report. South Korean media have reported that Washington asked that Seoul's National Intelligence Service be excluded from a June meeting with US and Japanese officials on North Korean cyber threats. Seoul's spy agency said the matter reflected a past misunderstanding and had been resolved, acknowledging restrictions on some intelligence connected to the earlier dispute but denying reports that the US had reduced sharing of North Korean missile information or cut the overall flow of intelligence. Kang said Seoul and Washington were discussing ways to secure South Korean rights to enrich uranium and reprocess spent nuclear fuel, either through revising their civil nuclear agreement or an additional arrangement. No progress had been made towards a summit between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, despite Trump signalling openness to dialogue, Kang said. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung told a cabinet meeting on Tuesday that Seoul should avoid subservient attitudes in dealings with other countries. Lee called the US alliance a central pillar of South Korean diplomacy which should be further developed, while adding that differences between countries were inevitable and should be managed through discussion and coordination.

The IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1 per cent, a slight uptick from the 3.0 per cent it predicted in July.

BANGKOK: The global economy will still manage to top 3 per cent real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday. Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above US$100 a barrel , the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1 per cent, a slight uptick from the 3.0 per cent it predicted in July. The World Economic Outlook forecast, released as global economic and finance leaders gather in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, is about even with the most optimistic scenario issued in April but below 2025 global growth of 3.5 per cent. For 2027, the IMF predicts 3.4 per cent global growth, flat with the July forecast and up 0.2 percentage points from April.

The slight improvement is largely due to continued strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, prompting growth upgrades for key advanced economies building AI platforms and especially for countries supplying AI hardware, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand, which is hosting the meetings this week. "The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from just coping to rebuilding," the IMF's chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, told a news conference. "We need to restore fiscal space. We need to rebuild supply-side resilience." She said major downside risks to growth include a prolonged, intensified war in the Middle East that spikes inflation pressures, rising bond yields that raise government borrowing costs, El Nino-driven extreme weather events and a reassessment of AI profitability that craters investment and asset prices. Countries and companies moved quickly to mitigate the oil price shock, drawing down reserves, substituting other suppliers and energy sources and cutting oil demand, Petya Koeva Brooks, the IMF's deputy research director, told Reuters in a separate interview. She said global growth would have fallen to 2.5 per cent this year without these measures, but their effect is fading as the war drags on. The IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95 per cent of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April. Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47 per cent of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains. Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran , with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3 per cent this year compared with the 1.7 per cent growth predicted in July. Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into deep recessions, with 2026 contractions of 7.6 per cent, 16 per cent, 16.7 per cent, 15.6 per cent and 3.9 per cent, respectively.

Related:

WTO lifts global trade outlook as AI boom powers Asian growth

WTO warns of 'most serious and sustained' trade disruptions

UNITED STATES FLAT, IMPROVEMENT IN EUROPE Among major economies, the IMF forecast US growth of 2.3 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, unchanged for this year and 0.1 percentage point higher for next year. The US economy is expected to be supported by robust private consumption, tax cuts and AI investment, though the boost from AI will be offset by its large import content. Eurozone growth for 2026 was upgraded to 1.1 per cent from 0.9 per cent in July due to stronger investment in AI, participation in AI value chains such as chemical production in Germany, and higher defence spending in EU countries. Britain's 2026 growth forecast also was upgraded by 0.3 percentage points from July to 1.3 per cent due to larger AI investment. The IMF forecast China's growth at 4.5 per cent for 2026 and 4.0 per cent for 2027, both down 0.1 percentage point from July, as higher oil prices exacerbate weak domestic demand despite strong exports. India remains the world's fastest-growing major economy at 7.0 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, up 0.6 percentage point this year and 0.3 percentage point next year compared with the July forecasts amid robust domestic demand, services activity and AI investment. The AI investment surge is projected to keep upward pressure on prices, with global headline consumer price inflation forecast at 4.7 per cent in 2026 and 4.1 per cent for 2027.

Related:

AI productivity gains may not curb inflation, IMF's Tenreyro warns

AI is creating an economy that can grow without needing more workers. Should we be worried?

ENERGY PRICE, AI RISKS Participants at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok will be assessing a precarious outlook. The IMF forecasts are based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 with a broad return to pre-war shipping conditions occurring by October 2027. The IMF assumes an average oil price of US$96 per barrel for 2026 and US$87 in 2027. But under an adverse scenario highlighted in the report, in which a worsening war pushes oil prices to US$130 per barrel through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be reduced by 0.2 percentage point in 2026 and 0.5 percentage point in 2027. Inflation in 2027 would surge by another 1.1 percentage point to 5.2 per cent. AI is also a huge source of uncertainty, with major downside and upside risks, the IMF report said. Under a scenario of faster adoption of the technology and accelerated investment, global GDP could rise a further 0.6 per cent by 2029, with the bulk of the benefits going to the US and China. But if productivity gains from AI fail to materialise, prompting a sharp decline in investment, US GDP could fall by 0.8 per cent directly, causing spillovers to Asian technology exporters with a total direct GDP impact of as much as 0.4 per cent by 2028. This shift would also trigger a sharp reduction in asset prices and tighter financial conditions that cause a major drop in consumption, particularly in the US, the IMF said. Higher global bond yields would further reduce activity, with a combined global output reduction of 1.1 per cent by 2028, including a 1.8 per cent drop in US output. The IMF also warned that elevated public debt levels, particularly in advanced economies, increase the risk of sharply higher borrowing costs that can weigh on growth prospects. It urged governments to stop delaying action to rebuild fiscal buffers and articulate credible medium-term plans to bring debt back to sustainable levels - advice that IMF officials plan to push at the Bangkok meetings.
